centralObject.name: The Paramount–states consent decree (N.D. Cal., Judge Martínez-Olguín, approved 2026-09-30) — five years of conduct terms that clear Paramount's takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery

place.why: The decree binds Paramount's management (theatrical output, lots, cable bundling, a newsroom board) while letting the merger close, which mainly presses on the pro-business right and leaves the anti-monopoly left without the structural remedy it wanted; its time limit and thin newsroom protection pull the read slightly negative.

tethers.title: Mergers that may substantially lessen competition; private and state suits for injunctive relief
tethers.why: The law the 12 states sued under (late July 2026); §16 is what let states sue after the Justice Department cleared the deal, and the decree is the remedy entered in that suit.

place.why: The decree is this statute's remedy here; it carries the decree's read.

tethers.title: Premerger notification and federal review
tethers.why: The federal review path: the Antitrust Division closed its review on 2026-06-12 with no divestitures or conditions, which is why the remedy came from the states instead.

place.why: The federal track that cleared the deal before the window; it neither delivers nor fails here.

title: Thirty Films a Year
prompt: A judge approved the states' deal with Paramount, and Warner Bros. is about to be absorbed. Do thirty films a year and a CNN board protect anything?
framing: On Wednesday, September 30, 2026, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Northern California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 states led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, clearing Paramount's takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery to close. The states had sued under federal antitrust law in July 2026; the Justice Department had cleared the deal without conditions on June 12, 2026. For five years, Paramount must release at least 30 films a year in theaters, raise U.S. film production spending, negotiate its cable channels separately from Warner's, keep an independent board for CBS News and CNN editorial disputes, and fund support for displaced workers. The judge called the decree "a reasonable factual and legal resolution" and rejected outside objections. Paramount is run by David Ellison; his father, Larry Ellison, a Trump ally, is financing the deal.

split.seam: Institutional vs populist (y): both institutional fluid stations read delivery positive because they trust the enforcer or the operator, and both populist fluid stations read it negative because the structure and ownership are untouched; at the rim, trust in Ellison/Trump pulls D across the seam.
split.rationale: Party (x) predicts less than y here: A and B agree the terms will be kept, and C and D agree they don't touch concentration. The fluid band splits cleanly on y, while the rim regroups by who trusts the Ellisons (B, D) and who trusts Bonta (A) against C.

zPattern.note: Centers are fluid z; coalition z: A −0.05, B −0.15, C −0.3, D −0.2. Fluid splits on y (A, B +; C, D −); every coalition sits just below zero. Rims sign by holder-trust exactly: A trusts Bonta, B the Ellisons, D 'Trump's people' (+); C distrusts Ellison and Trump (−). D's rim crosses its own fluid sign.

antiValentRationale: At D's rim the sign flips from its own fluid read (−0.55 to +0.4), because a trusted Trump-allied owner replaces the anti-Big-Media argument, and B's rim rises well above its coalition doubts; holder-trust inverts the merits read in exactly the band where the object drops out.

z.pos: the decree delivers: its commitments keep films, jobs and newsroom independence in place for five years, and enforcement has teeth
z.neg: it doesn't: the merger goes through, the terms are thin and time-limited, and the concentration and political ownership of CNN and CBS go unchecked

fluid.zReason: A court-enforced decree with a $30 million penalty for each missing film, 45-day windows and a ban on selling or closing the lots makes compliance cheaper than default for five years.

instrument.holder: the federal court and the state AGs

fluid.text: Thirty films a year, then thirty-two, with $30 million on the line for every one they skip. That's not a press release, that's a number a judge can collect. The DOJ waved this through with nothing, so I'll count the lots staying open as a real win.

coalition.zReason: The terms protect California's production base, which is what the brokers needed, but they don't touch the concentration that Letitia James and William Tong said was the actual problem.
coalition.text: I defended this all week, and then I noticed who pushed hardest for it: the governor and the mayor, worried about the studio leaving for Texas. The people I vote with got jobs in LA and called it antitrust. James and Tong aren't wrong that nobody touched the size of the thing.

denominated.zReason: Trust in Bonta stands in for the terms.
denominated.text: Bonta fought for this and he said it protects competition. That's enough for me.

fluid.zReason: Paramount's management has the scale and the cash to meet the film quota and production commitments, so the terms will be met, even if they are state-imposed industrial policy.
fluid.text: The Justice Department reviewed this for eight months and found nothing to fix, and then twelve states rewrote a business plan anyway. Will Paramount hit thirty films? Sure, it needs the scale to take on Netflix and Disney, and the penalties are easy to see coming. My problem is twelve states writing a studio's business plan, not whether the promises get kept.

coalition.zReason: A five-member board with no ownership power can't hold out against an owner that political friends want to reshape CNN, and the free-market side has stopped caring about rules when the buyer is an ally.
coalition.text: The people I vote with spent years warning about media conglomerates, and now they're cheering one because Larry Ellison is a friend of the president. If I wouldn't trust a five-person board to check an owner I disliked, why would I pretend it checks one I like? Foreign money owning nearly half of it doesn't sit right with me either.

denominated.zReason: Trust in the Ellisons stands in for the terms.
denominated.text: Larry Ellison builds things that work. If the Ellisons signed it, they'll deliver.

fluid.zReason: Conduct terms that expire in five years leave the merger itself, and a Trump ally's control of CNN and CBS News, permanently in place.
fluid.text: Five years of movie quotas, and then Warner Bros. is gone for good. A five-member board doesn't own anything; the Ellisons do, and the money behind them comes from a Trump ally. Why does the merger last forever when the protections don't?

coalition.zReason: The worker fund and the ban on closing the lots give guild members something a blocked suit might not have, which narrows the gap between this deal and a loss in court.
coalition.text: I keep calling it a sellout, but the people I organize with need the lots open and the displaced-worker fund paid, and a lawsuit that loses gets them nothing. Maybe my side wanted a scalp more than a paycheck. Still, I'm not calling a layoff cushion antitrust.

denominated.zReason: Distrust of Ellison and Trump stands in for the terms.
denominated.text: Trump's billionaire just bought CNN. A board isn't going to stop that.

fluid.zReason: The decree regulates California output and jobs instead of market structure, so the giant still gets bigger and the newsroom board is just a guarantee written by blue-state AGs.
fluid.text: Twelve blue states set a quota for Hollywood and called it competition. HBO Max, Paramount+, CNN and CBS all under one roof, and the fix is a theater count? The CNN board just lets Sacramento babysit the newsroom.

coalition.zReason: The board may keep CNN from changing much, but if the populist right is betting on new ownership to fix CNN, it is counting on the same concentration it says it opposes.
coalition.text: The people I vote with hated Big Media until a Trump-friendly family bought the biggest piece of it. Now they're hoping the new owner cleans up CNN, and the board's the only thing in the way. I don't like the board, but I'm not sure I like what I'm rooting for either.

denominated.zReason: Trust in Trump's camp stands in for the terms.
denominated.text: Trump's guy owns CNN now. That's the only protection I care about.

objectLayer.stated: An antitrust remedy: conduct commitments (theatrical output, production spending, separate cable negotiation, a CBS News/CNN editorial board, worker support) that protect competition for five years.
objectLayer.operative: The price of letting the merger close. No divestiture; behavioral terms with a five-year life, policed by the states and the court. The operative fight is over who owns CNN and CBS News, which the decree touches only through a board.
objectLayer.inversion: Lean, not ruled: at the right rims, holder-trust in a Trump-allied owner replaces the right-populist anti-Big-Media read (D −0.55 fluid → +0.4 rim). No cited prior; see meta.newsroomFindings.
